idea_chosen.hook: It isn't UGC. It's Player-Generated Content - and that difference is the whole business.
idea_chosen.angle: PLAY3's own category, PGC (Player-Generated Content), is not the same as generic UGC - the distinction (real player, own avatar, own feed, brand template, full attribution) is the whole business model and has never been argued directly in this pipeline.
idea_chosen.audience: Brand marketers/CMOs evaluating gaming/virtual-world content strategy

copy.body:
It isn't UGC. It's Player-Generated Content — and that difference is the whole business.

Most marketers hear "UGC" and think of a hashtag campaign: unpaid creators posting because a brand asked nicely, tagged with a branded hashtag, counted as impressions. It's borrowed enthusiasm from someone who owes you nothing after the post goes up.

PGC is a different mechanism entirely. A real player, inside a brand's own Roblox experience, makes a video starring their own avatar. They post it to their own TikTok or YouTube feed — the player's account, not the brand's — and the brand still gets full attribution back to the campaign. Ownership doesn't get lost between the creative and the tracking.

That distinction is the whole business model, not a marketing nuance. Renting a creator's audience for a post ends when the invoice clears. Earning a player's actual attention compounds. The content keeps circulating on their feed, in their voice, long after the campaign budget stops.

Here's the receipt: one five-day activation generated 16,371 conversations about a single beanie. Not impressions. Not views. Conversations — real players talking to each other and to a brand agent about one product, unprompted.

If your team is still reporting on UGC volume instead of who made it, where it lives, and what it's attributed to, what number are you actually optimizing for?
